extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for observing and interpreting dress, facial features, gestures, and body language of accused, witnesses, jurors and others in legal settings to draw inferences about truthfulness, emotion, resolve, and character. Emphasizes Darwinian principles, careful observation, and distinguishing genuine from simulated expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress/clothing as indicator of character
rubrics_metrics.description: A man’s general appearance and way of dressing indicate refinement, attention to particulars, and character traits; clothing frequently yields reliable inferences about honesty, social type, and inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider habitual dress patterns rather than single oddities; account for possible temporary influences (economic compulsion, passing inclination) but note these influences are often shallow. Examples: an honest farm hand would not wear a dress-coat; discharged soldiers, hunters, officials have characteristic dress. Use dress as one cue among many, not definitive alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single item of dress betrays character
rubrics_metrics.description: Often a single item of dress can betray a person’s character or social type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore single distinctive items (e.g., shabby elegance, suggestive dress); they may be as informative as the whole costume. Treat as corroborative evidence to other observational cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing groups reflect social/national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothes of groups (soldiers, hunters, officials, clerics, political types) are well-defined and reveal group character much like national dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition of group-typical attire to form initial, provisional inferences about role and disposition; avoid overgeneralizing from dress alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy as readable features
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain spiritual qualities (intelligence, kindness, cruelty, foolishness) can be read from facial features; the simplest valid generalizations should be extendable and examinable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiognomy has variable value and must be built only on careful observation, avoiding exaggeration and unfounded assertions. Collect empirical data and beware of dogmatic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physiognomy, mimicry, and phrenology
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiognomy concerns facial features and their relation to traits; mimicry concerns voluntary alterations of expression and gesture; phrenology concerns skull conformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply physiognomy to features and involuntary expressions; mimicry is more relevant to actors/orators and is often voluntary; understand which domain an observed movement belongs to before inferring inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer studying children and unstudied persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Children and simple, unstudied persons provide clear, vigorous, and uncontrived expressions useful as paradigms for mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations of children and unspoiled peasants to establish baseline meanings of expressions, then apply mutatis mutandis to adults while accounting for masking and learned concealment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian principle: purposeful associated habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated voluntary actions associated with desires or states can become inherited or habitual reflexes, producing recurrent expressions and gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret many stereotyped expressions (e.g., nodding, eyebrow movement) as habitual outcomes of recurrent mental states; use these habitual associations to read likely internal states, but check for idiosyncratic habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian principle: antithesis (contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictory mental states often produce contrasting gestures (antithesis) that clarify meaning—for example, shrugging opposite firmness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe oppositional gesture pairs to infer intended affect or attitude; consider cultural or institutional gesture-languages (e.g., monastic antithesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian principle: direct nervous activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain expressions (pal­ing, trembling, pupil changes, blushing, sweating, tears) arise directly from nervous activity and are less volitionally controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these involuntary responses as particularly diagnostic of intense emotions (fear, pain, joy); they are harder to simulate convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware accidental or habitual meaningless movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many muscle movements occur accidentally or from unrelated pains/habits and have no significance for emotional states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-interpret isolated, idiosyncratic movements. Corroborate with other cues and context; distinguish transient accidental motions from patterned responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of eye closure: exclusion vs recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief eye-closure when shown evidence often signals desire to exclude consequences (short, fear-accompanied), whereas long eye-closure may indicate deliberate recollection or collection of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish short defensive closures (indicative of fear/avoidance and potential concealment) from longer closures for mental review; note accompanying facial and hand gestures (short closure often accompanied by defensive hand movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive hand movement accompanying brief eye closure
rubrics_metrics.description: When eyes are closed briefly to exclude consequences, a contemporary defensive hand movement is often present and observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/timing of the hand movement to differentiate exclusionary eye-closing from reflective eye-closing; this increases reliability of interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction between gestures and words is diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person’s gestures contradict their words (e.g., closes eyes while contesting evidence), the contradiction is suggestive and legally significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize observed contradictions as evidence of concealment, fear, or oversharing; follow up immediately (appeal to conscience, probe further) when a brief exclusionary closure accompanies contesting language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed mouth and lip-pressing indicate resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden closing of the mouth and pressed lips accompany firm resolution; such gestures often precede decisive verbal acts (confession, refusal to answer, sticking to a denial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret abrupt mouth-closing as a sign that a definite resolution has been reached; anticipate that subsequent speech will follow that decision and may be difficult to alter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation of jurymen’s resolution predicts votes
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of resolution in jurymen (e.g., characteristic gestures) commonly indicate that they have decided how to vote and are unlikely to be converted by further testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced observers may count votes by noting these signs; be aware that resolved jurors may hear subsequent evidence selectively and prejudicially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astonishment gestures and their form
rubrics_metrics.description: Astonishment is expressed by hands raised, palm laid on mouth, raised eyebrows, forehead beating, and a slight winding movement of the trunk (often leftward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these gestures to detect surprise that has been suppressed verbally; particularly significant when the person ought to be astonished but attempts to hide it—revealing a telling reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorn gestures and detection of simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scorn manifests via nasal and oral movements (nose contraction, creases), sniffing/spitting/blowing, folded arms, and raised shoulders; simulated scorn is often accompanied by unnecessary smiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish real scorn (no gratuitous smile, natural posture) from theatrical scorn (exaggeration, forced smile). Real scorn tends to be less performative and more congruent with context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defiance and spite gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Defiance and spite show in baring canine teeth, drawing the face into a frown toward the object, closed mouth, and several forced nasal exhalations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combine resolution and scorn; treat such defendants as challenging and often embittered. Handle with patient, earnest discussion rather than escalation; consider possibility of innocence masked by embitterment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision/depreciation as milder defiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Derision and depreciation display similar expressions to defiance and spite but in a lesser degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret as milder contempt; apply similar cautions about simulation and context but expect less intensity and commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of real rage
rubrics_metrics.description: Real rage: body erect or thrown forward, stiff limbs, mouth and teeth closely pressed, voice very loud or hoarse, wrinkled forehead, contracted pupil, and color changes (flush or pallor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real rage is rarely convincingly simulated and the cluster of signs usually makes recognition reliable. Treat such displays seriously but attempt calm management; be aware of potential injustice if rage is misread as consciousness of guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guilty sparkle and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'guilty sparkle' in the eyes — an intensified tear secretion — can indicate nervous excitation from guilt; by contrast, persons who know themselves guilty may show affectation to conceal it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish naive natural behavior (no artifice) from affected behavior (theatrical, overdone). Note that innocent naive people often display naturalness; affectedness can betray concealment attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation gesture: folding hands in lap
rubrics_metrics.description: Folding the hands in the lap is a proverbial sign of resignation—an acceptance of 'there is nothing more to be done'—and indicates surrender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resignation can be shown by both innocent and guilty people, but genuine resignation implying cession of a claimed right is more typical of the innocent or those who have accepted unavoidable consequences. Contextualize with surrounding evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction of the brow: multiple meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Brow contraction can indicate intensive consideration (requiring acuter vision), disgust, or disbelief—especially when combined with a smile (disbelief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate earnest intensive thinking (accompanied by other signs of concentration and memory search) from simulated thought (mere imitation) and from disgust. For alibi questioning, real brow contraction with other memory signs suggests genuine recollection; simulated contraction without accompanying signs suggests deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank stare: absorption and opportunity for confession
rubrics_metrics.description: A blank expression or vacant stare indicates that a person is lost in thought or engaged in intuitive recollection, not necessarily active analytical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This state often yields opportunities for confession if leveraged sensitively (allowing them to continue in reflective silence); do not confuse blank stare with deliberate evasion—note the absence of distinguishing gestures unless embarrassment occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect theatrical/over-exaggerated simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulated emotions and gestures are often theatrical, exaggerated, or attended by unnecessary smiling and unnatural poses that betray artificiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to recognize over-exaggeration, theatricality, and incongruent smiles as markers of simulation; cross-check with involuntary signs (pupil changes, blushing, trembling) and with context to avoid false positives.
